title: Physics — The motor effect

final_note: You worked through Physics — The motor effect — 20 specification statements.

concepts.def: Whenever a current flows in a conducting wire, a magnetic field is produced in the space around the wire. The field exists only while the current flows: switch the current off and the field disappears.

concepts.term: Field pattern around a straight wire
concepts.def: The field lines around a long straight current-carrying wire are concentric circles lying in a plane at right angles to the wire and centred on it. The circles are drawn close together near the wire and further apart further away, showing that the field is strongest close to the wire.

concepts.term: Factors affecting the field around a wire
concepts.def: The strength of the magnetic field around a wire depends on two things: the current through the wire, and the distance from the wire. A larger current gives a stronger field; moving further from the wire gives a weaker field.

concepts.term: Direction of the field around a wire
concepts.def: The direction of the circular field lines is shown by arrowheads and is given by the right-hand grip rule: point the right thumb along the conventional current and the curled fingers give the direction of the field lines. Reversing the current reverses every arrow.

A solenoid is a wire wound into a long coil of many turns. Shaping the wire this way increases the strength of the magnetic field produced by a given current, because the field of each turn adds to the field of its neighbours.

Inside a current-carrying solenoid the magnetic field is strong and uniform: the same strength and direction everywhere inside the coil. It is drawn as straight, evenly spaced, parallel lines running along the axis of the coil.

Outside the coil the field spreads out and has a similar shape to the field of a bar magnet, with one end of the solenoid behaving as a north pole and the other as a south pole. The lines outside run from the north end round to the south end, and every line is a closed loop that continues through the inside of the coil.

A core of iron placed inside a solenoid is magnetised by the field of the coil and greatly increases the strength of the magnetic field. Iron is used because it loses almost all of its magnetism as soon as the current is switched off.
An electromagnet is a solenoid with an iron core. Its magnetic field can be switched on and off with the current, and its strength can be changed by changing the current or the number of turns.

The magnetic effect of a current is demonstrated by placing plotting compasses, or scattering iron filings, near a wire and switching the current on: the compasses swing round to lie end to end along circles around the wire, and swing back to north when the current is switched off.

The magnetic effect of a current can be increased by increasing the current, by winding the wire into a solenoid with more turns so that the fields of the turns add together, and by adding an iron core.

In a relay a small current in a coil magnetises an iron core, which attracts a pivoted iron armature; the armature closes contacts in a second, separate circuit. A small current can therefore switch on a much larger one, and the two circuits stay electrically isolated from each other.

In an electric bell the current passes through an electromagnet that attracts an iron armature carrying a hammer; as the armature moves it breaks the circuit, the electromagnet switches off, a spring pulls the armature back and the circuit is remade, so the hammer strikes repeatedly.
When a conductor carrying a current is placed in a magnetic field, the magnet producing the field and the conductor exert a force on each other. This is called the motor effect.

Hold the thumb, first finger and second finger of the left hand at right angles to one another. The First finger points along the Field, the seCond finger along the Current, and the thuMb then gives the direction of the force, that is the Motion of the conductor.

concepts.term: Factors affecting the size of the force
concepts.def: The size of the force on a conductor in a magnetic field depends on the magnetic flux density of the field, the current through the conductor, and the length of conductor that is inside the field.
Magnetic flux density, symbol B, is the measure of the strength of a magnetic field used in this equation. It is measured in tesla, T, and a stronger magnet gives a larger flux density.
For a conductor at right angles to a magnetic field and carrying a current: force = magnetic flux density × current × length, written in symbols as F = B I l.
The tesla, T, is the unit of magnetic flux density. A flux density of 1 T gives a force of 1 N on each metre of a conductor carrying a current of 1 A at right angles to the field.

concepts.term: Symbols and units in F = B I l
concepts.def: Force, F, in newtons, N; magnetic flux density, B, in tesla, T; current, I, in amperes, A (amp is acceptable for ampere); length, l, in metres, m. Values must be substituted in these units, so a length given in centimetres has to be converted to metres first.

A coil of wire carrying a current in a magnetic field tends to rotate, because the forces on its two opposite sides act in opposite directions and so turn the coil about its axle. This is the basis of an electric motor.

The split-ring commutator reverses the direction of the current in the coil every half turn, just as the coil passes the vertical. The forces on the two sides therefore swap over at the right moment, and the coil keeps rotating in the same direction instead of stopping and rocking back.

mcqs.q: A long straight vertical wire carries a steady current. What is the shape of the magnetic field pattern around the wire?
options: Circles centred on the wire and lying in a plane at right angles to it
Straight lines that spread out from the wire, like spokes on a wheel
Straight lines running parallel to the wire along its whole length
Loops that leave one end of the wire and enter at the other end
mcqs.explain: The field around a straight current-carrying wire is a set of concentric circles perpendicular to it.

mcqs.q: A plotting compass is moved from 2 cm to 6 cm away from a wire carrying a steady current. The current is not changed. What happens to the deflection of the compass?
options: It stays the same, because the current through the wire is unchanged
It falls to zero, because the field stops at the outer circle
It gets smaller, because the field is weaker further from the wire
It gets larger, because the field circles are wider further out
mcqs.explain: Field strength depends on distance from the wire as well as on the current, so it falls as the compass is moved away.

mcqs.q: A student winds a straight wire into a solenoid and passes the same current through it as before. What happens to the magnetic field produced?
options: It is weaker, because the current now has a longer path to run
It is stronger, because the fields of the turns add together
It is unchanged, because the current in the wire is unchanged
There is no field at all until an iron core is in the coil
mcqs.explain: Shaping a wire into a solenoid increases the strength of the field, because each turn adds its field to its neighbours'.

mcqs.q: What best describes the magnetic field inside a long solenoid that is carrying a current?
options: Strong at the very centre of the coil and almost zero elsewhere
A set of circles running round the axis, as around a straight wire
Weak inside the coil and strongest just outside the windings
Strong and uniform, drawn as evenly spaced parallel lines
mcqs.explain: The specification states that the field inside a solenoid is strong and uniform, so the lines are parallel and evenly spaced.

mcqs.q: How does the magnetic field around the outside of a current-carrying solenoid compare with that of a bar magnet?
options: It is a set of circles around the middle of the coil, not like a bar magnet
It has a similar shape, with one end acting as a north pole and one as a south
It has exactly the same shape, but the ends of a solenoid are not poles
There is no field outside the coil, so no comparison can be made
mcqs.explain: The specification states that the field around a solenoid has a similar shape to that of a bar magnet.

mcqs.q: An iron core is placed inside a solenoid that is carrying a current. What is the effect?
options: The solenoid begins to produce a magnetic field for the first time
The field grows stronger and stays on after the current is off
The core carries a current of its own that adds to the field
The magnetic field of the solenoid becomes considerably stronger
mcqs.explain: Adding an iron core increases the strength of the magnetic field of a solenoid; the arrangement is an electromagnet.

mcqs.q: Which observation best demonstrates that a current in a wire produces a magnetic field?
options: A compass beside the wire swings round when the current is switched on
A plotting compass beside the wire keeps pointing north when the current is off
The wire becomes noticeably warmer when the current is switched on
A piece of copper wire placed beside the wire is pulled sideways towards it
mcqs.explain: The compass responds only to a magnetic field, and it moves exactly when the current begins, so the current is the cause.

mcqs.q: The direction of the current in a straight wire is reversed. What happens to the magnetic field pattern?
options: The pattern and the arrows on it are both completely unchanged
The circles turn into straight lines pointing back along the wire
The circles stay, but the arrows point the other way round
The circles are replaced by a bar-magnet pattern with swapped poles
mcqs.explain: The pattern is fixed by the shape of the wire and the direction by the direction of the current, so only the arrows reverse.

mcqs.q: A student is asked to draw the magnetic field of a current-carrying solenoid, showing its direction. Which drawing is correct?
options: Parallel lines inside the coil and loops outside it, with no arrows on any line
Parallel arrows inside the coil that start at one end and stop at the other
Closely spaced parallel arrows inside the coil, looping outside from north to south
Circles drawn around the outside of the coil, with clockwise arrows shown
mcqs.explain: Inside the coil the field is uniform and along the axis; outside, each line loops back, giving the bar-magnet shape.

mcqs.q: Why does winding a wire into a solenoid increase the magnetic effect of the current?
options: The field of each turn points the same way inside the coil, so they add up
Winding the wire into a coil increases the current flowing in it
The coiled wire has a much larger resistance, and that strengthens the field
The turns of wire trap the field lines so that none can escape the coil
mcqs.explain: Many turns contribute their fields at the same place and in the same direction, so the total field is much stronger.

mcqs.q: A relay diagram shows a coil wound on an iron core in one circuit, and a pivoted iron armature that closes contacts in a second circuit. How does the relay work?
options: The current in the coil flows on through the contacts and into the second circuit
The magnetised iron core repels the armature and pushes it onto the contacts
The coil heats the armature, which bends until it touches the contacts
A small current magnetises the core, so the armature closes the contacts
mcqs.explain: The coil's magnetic effect moves the armature, so a small current in one circuit switches on a separate circuit.

mcqs.q: A wire carrying a current is held at right angles to the field between the poles of a magnet. Which statement about the forces is correct?
options: Only the wire feels a force, as the magnet carries no current
The magnet and the wire each exert a force on the other
Only the magnet feels a force, because it produces the field
Neither feels a force until the wire is free to move about
mcqs.explain: The specification states that the magnet producing the field and the conductor exert a force on each other.

mcqs.q: In Fleming's left-hand rule, what do the first finger, the second finger and the thumb represent?
options: The first finger is the current, the second the field, the thumb the motion
The first finger is the force, the second the field, and the thumb current
The right hand is used, with the field, current and force in that order
The first finger the field, the second finger the current, and the thumb the force
mcqs.explain: First finger Field, seCond finger Current, thuMb Motion: the three are held at right angles to one another.

mcqs.q: A horizontal wire carries a current from left to right. The magnetic field between the poles is directed into the page. In which direction is the force on the wire?
options: Downwards, at right angles to both the field and the current
Upwards, at right angles to both the current and the field
Into the page, in the same direction as the field itself
To the right, in the same direction as the current
mcqs.explain: First finger into the page and second finger to the right puts the thumb, and so the force, upwards.

mcqs.q: Which change would increase the size of the force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field?
options: Using much longer connecting leads between the cell and the wire
Using a much longer wire, most of it outside the field
Using a stronger magnet, so that the flux density is larger
Reducing the current so that less energy is lost as heat
mcqs.explain: The force depends on the magnetic flux density, the current and the length of conductor in the field.

mcqs.q: A straight wire carrying a current is placed so that it lies along the magnetic field lines. What is the force on the wire?
options: Zero, because the wire is not at right angles to the field
The largest possible force, as the wire lies along the field
Exactly the same force as when the wire is at right angles to it
A force along the wire, in the direction of the current in it
mcqs.explain: The equation applies to a conductor at right angles to the field; a wire lying along the field feels no force.

mcqs.q: For a conductor at right angles to a magnetic field and carrying a current, which word equation gives the force on the conductor?
options: force = magnetic field strength × current × length
force = magnetic flux density × charge × length
force = magnetic flux density × current × length
force = magnetic flux density × current × time
mcqs.explain: This is the equation as the specification states it, for a conductor at right angles to the field.

mcqs.q: In the equation F = B I l, what do the symbols B and l stand for?
options: B is the magnetic flux density and l is the length of conductor in the field
B is the magnetic flux density and l is the length of the whole circuit
B is the number of field lines drawn and l is the length of the wire
B is the force from the magnet and l is the length of the conductor
mcqs.explain: B is the flux density in tesla and l is the length of the conductor that lies inside the field, in metres.

mcqs.q: Which set of units should be used when the equation F = B I l is applied?
options: F in newtons, B in newtons, I in amperes and l in metres
F in newtons, B in tesla, I in volts and l in centimetres
F in joules, B in tesla, I in amperes and l in metres
F in newtons, B in tesla, I in amperes and l in metres
mcqs.explain: These are the units given in the specification: force in newtons, flux density in tesla, current in amperes, length in metres.

mcqs.q: A wire of length 0.30 m lies at right angles to a magnetic field of flux density 0.20 T. The current in the wire is 2.0 A. What is the force on the wire?
mcqs.explain: F = B I l = 0.20 × 2.0 × 0.30 = 0.12 N, with the length already in metres.

mcqs.q: A wire of length 0.30 m carries a current of 8.0 A at right angles to a magnetic field. The force on the wire is 4.8 N. What is the magnetic flux density?
mcqs.explain: Rearranging gives B = F ÷ (I × l) = 4.8 ÷ (8.0 × 0.30) = 2.0 T.

mcqs.q: A rectangular coil carrying a current is mounted on an axle between the poles of a magnet. Why does the coil tend to rotate?
options: The forces on both of its sides act in the same direction, pushing it
The coil becomes a magnet and is pulled towards the north pole
The forces on its opposite sides act in opposite directions
The current warms the coil, which expands and turns on its axle
mcqs.explain: The current runs opposite ways along the two sides, so the forces on them are opposite and turn the coil.

mcqs.q: In a simple d.c. motor, what is the job of the split-ring commutator?
options: It carries the current into the coil, so that a force can act on the coil
It reverses the current in the coil every half turn, so it keeps turning one way
It reverses the magnetic field every half turn, so the coil keeps going
It holds the coil steady so that it turns at a constant rate of spin
mcqs.explain: Swapping the connections as the coil passes the vertical swaps the two forces over and keeps the rotation going.
